segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jude, a slave of Jesus Christ and a brother of James, to those who are called, loved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: May mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Beloved, while I was making every effort to write to you about the salvation we share, I found it necessary to write and urge you to contend for the faith that was handed down to the holy ones once for all.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For certain people have slipped in unnoticed, those who were long ago written down for this condemnation, ungodly people who turn the grace of our God into debauchery and deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now I want to remind you, though you know all of this once for all, that Jesus, having saved a people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and the angels who did not keep their own domain but abandoned their proper dwelling he has kept in everlasting chains beneath the gloom for the judgment of the great day;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: just as Sodom and Gomorrah and the cities around them, which in the same way as these gave themselves over to sexual immorality and went after flesh of a different kind, stand as an example, undergoing the punishment of eternal fire.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Yet in the same way these people too, in their dreaming, defile the flesh, reject lordship, and slander the glorious ones.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Michael the archangel, when he was disputing with the devil and arguing about the body of Moses, did not dare to bring a slanderous judgment against him, but said,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “May the Lord rebuke you!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But these people slander whatever they do not understand, and whatever they do know by instinct, like unreasoning animals, by these things they are ruined.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Woe to them! For they have gone the way of Cain, have abandoned themselves to Balaam’s error for pay, and have perished in Korah’s rebellion.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: These are the reefs at your love feasts, feasting with you, fearlessly shepherding themselves; waterless clouds swept along by winds; late-autumn trees without fruit, twice dead, uprooted;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: wild waves of the sea, foaming up their own shameful deeds; wandering stars, for whom the gloom of darkness has been kept forever.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It was about these people too that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Look, the Lord comes with his holy myriads,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: to execute judgment on all, and to convict all the ungodly of all the ungodly deeds they committed in their ungodliness, and of all the harsh things that ungodly sinners have spoken against him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: These people are grumblers, complainers about their lot, following their own desires; their mouths speak bombast, and they flatter people for the sake of gain.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But you, beloved, remember the words spoken beforehand by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for they used to say to you,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “In the last time there will be scoffers, following their own ungodly desires.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: These are the ones who cause divisions, merely natural people who do not have the Spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But you, beloved, building yourselves up on your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: keep yourselves in the love of God, as you wait for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And have mercy on some, those who are wavering;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: save others, snatching them out of the fire; and on others have mercy with fear, hating even the tunic stained by the flesh.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now to the one who is able to guard you from stumbling and to make you stand in the presence of his glory without blemish and with great joy,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to the only God, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, might, and authority, before every age and now and for all the ages. Amen.

notes.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master, and a first-century reader would have heard it that way. Most English versions soften it to 'servant', partly because 'slave of God' was also an honorific in the Septuagint for figures such as Moses and David. Both the ownership and the honour are probably in view here.

notes.traditional: kept for Jesus Christ; preserved in Jesus Christ
notes.note: The Greek has a bare dative, which can mean 'kept for Jesus Christ' (safe until his coming) or 'kept by Jesus Christ'. Most recent translations choose 'for'. The verb 'keep' recurs through the letter (verses 6, 13, 21) and is rendered the same way each time.

The traditional 'saints' now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek term is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'God's people'.

The manuscripts are divided here: some read 'Jesus', many read 'the Lord', and a few read 'God'. The Greek edition translated here adopts 'Jesus', the harder reading and one with strong early support, which would mean Jude sees Jesus as active in the exodus. Most older English versions follow 'the Lord'. The position of 'once for all' in the sentence also varies among manuscripts.

notes.phrase: the angels who did not keep their own domain
notes.note: Jude alludes to a Jewish tradition, built on Genesis 6:1–4 and told at length in 1 Enoch, in which angels left heaven to take human wives and were imprisoned until the final judgment. His readers evidently knew the story. The word rendered 'domain' can also mean 'position of authority' or 'rule'.

The Greek is literally 'other flesh' or 'different flesh'. Many translations paraphrase it as 'unnatural desire' or 'perversion'. The literal wording fits the comparison Jude is drawing: 'these' most naturally refers to the angels of verse 6, who crossed the boundary between angels and humans, as the men of Sodom sought to do with their angelic visitors (Genesis 19). Some interpreters instead take the phrase as a reference to same-sex acts.

The Greek is literally 'glories', a term used in Jewish writings for angelic beings. Most scholars take it that way here, which explains the example of Michael that follows. Older versions rendered it 'dignities', which could suggest human authorities.

This episode is not in the Old Testament. Early Christian writers say Jude drew it from a Jewish work about the death of Moses, the relevant part of which has not survived. Michael's words echo Zechariah 3:2, where the Lord rebukes Satan.

The Greek word normally means a rock in or under the sea, a hazard to ships, and that is the sense followed here. Many translations instead render 'blemishes' or 'spots', taking it as equivalent to a similar word used in the parallel at 2 Peter 2:13. Both readings have scholarly support. The 'love feasts' were the shared meals of the early Christian communities.

The quotation is from 1 Enoch 1:9, a Jewish work widely read in this period but not part of most biblical canons. Enoch is counted seventh from Adam by inclusive reckoning of the generations in Genesis 5. The verb rendered 'comes' is a past tense in the Greek, a prophetic way of speaking of a future event as certain.

The Greek adjective describes someone living at the level of ordinary human life, as opposed to life animated by God's Spirit; Paul uses it the same way in 1 Corinthians 2:14. 'Sensual' wrongly suggests bodily indulgence, and 'worldly' is vaguer than the Greek. Most interpreters take 'Spirit' here as the Holy Spirit.

The manuscripts of verses 22–23 differ considerably. Some have two groups of people and others three, and in place of the first 'have mercy' some read 'convince' or 'refute'. The three-group text translated here is the one most modern editions adopt, but the original wording is uncertain.

The same Greek verb is used in verse 9 of Michael 'disputing' with the devil. Here it may likewise mean 'those who dispute', or, as most translations take it, 'those who doubt' or 'waver'. An older tradition, following a different manuscript reading, renders 'making a distinction'.

candidates.reason: Occurs throughout the New Testament and translations split between 'slave' and 'servant', so readers need one consistent policy, especially in self-designations of apostles.
Frequent address in the letters, rendered variously 'beloved', 'dear friends', 'loved ones'; variation would obscure its link with the ἀγάπη word group.
Covers both abusive speech against people or angels and irreverence toward God; 'blaspheme', 'slander' and 'revile' need a principled split across books.
Rare but theologically weighty (1 Corinthians 2:14; 15:44–46; James 3:15; Jude 19) and rendered very differently ('natural', 'unspiritual', 'worldly', 'sensual').
Recurs in vice lists across the Gospels and letters with renderings ranging from 'sensuality' to 'licentiousness' to 'debauchery'.
